displayQuote: What is to give light must endure burning

meta.title: Who really said "What is to give light must endure burning"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Viktor Frankl. He quoted it and credited the poet in the same sentence: it closes Anton Wildgans's 1916 sonnet "Helldunkle Stunde".
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'What is to give light must endure burning'?
meta.ogDescription: Frankl quoted the line and named Anton Wildgans in the same breath. It closes Wildgans's 1916 sonnet, published in Mittag (1917).

answer.label: Not Viktor Frankl — actually Anton Wildgans
answer.sourceLine: The line closes “Helldunkle Stunde,” a sonnet Wildgans wrote in 1916 and published in his 1917 collection Mittag: “Was leuchten soll, muß dulden, daß es brennt.” Frankl really did quote it — and credited Wildgans by name in the same sentence. The familiar English wording is Richard and Clara Winston’s translation of Frankl’s book, where it reads “‘What is to give light must endure burning,’ Wildgans says.” Readers kept the sentence and dropped the attribution inside it.

source.heading: The sonnet it closes

docMeta.dd: Written 1916; first published in the collection Mittag, 1917
Ärztliche Seelsorge (1946), in English The Doctor and the Soul
Richard and Clara Winston, The Doctor and the Soul (Knopf, first English edition 1955)

source.excerpt:
Der ist zu sehr bewegtes Element,
Um, was nicht Licht ist, spiegelnd festzuhalten.
Nur, was sich flammenhaft vom Fleische trennt

In schmerzlichem und betendem Gestalten,
Vermag als unser Bildnis fortzuwalten.
Was leuchten soll, muß dulden, daß es brennt.
trail: The poet’s official site prints the sonnet in full and dates it precisely: “Geschrieben 1916; Erstveröffentlichung im Gedichtband ‚Mittag‘ 1917” ↗, ending “Was leuchten soll, muß dulden, daß es brennt.”
The same closing line appears in the scanned Gesammelte Werke, vol. 1 (1930) ↗ on p. 183, inside the “Gesänge im Mittag” cycle.

Frankl’s German text reads “…leuchten soll, muß dulden, daß es brennt’, sagt WILDGANS…” and the English translation “‘What is to give light must endure burning,’ Wildgans says” — both retrievable by searching inside the books ↗.

Wikiquote’s editors reached the same conclusion, noting the quote is widely credited to Frankl but “probably not” his ↗ and pointing to Wildgans’s poem. Quote Investigator has not published on this line.
source.excerptNote: The circulating English sentence renders only the final line. The tercets before it carry the argument: life is too restless a surface to reflect anything that is not light, so only what separates from the flesh flame-like, in painful and prayerful shaping, survives as our image.

source.rightsNote: Two different clocks run here. Wildgans’s German poem was published in 1917 and is in the public domain in the United States, and Wildgans died in 1932, so the original is free to reproduce. The famous English eight words are not the poem — they are Richard and Clara Winston’s rendering inside The Doctor and the Soul, first published by Knopf in 1955, and that translation remains in copyright.

author.name: Anton Wildgans
author.heading: Who was Anton Wildgans?
author.metaLine: 1881–1932 · Austrian poet, playwright and twice director of the Vienna Burgtheater
author.bio: Anton Wildgans was an Austrian poet and dramatist whose work blends realism, neo-romanticism and expressionism around the ordinary human condition. His plays Armut (1914), Liebe (1916) and Dies Irae (1918) made his name, and he twice directed Vienna’s Burgtheater, in 1921–1922 and again in 1930–1931. He is almost unknown to English readers — which is exactly why a single line of his has spent decades travelling under somebody else’s name.

misattribution.heading: Why Frankl’s name is on it
misattribution.intro: This is not a fabrication and not a paraphrase. The sentence is real, the English wording is real, and Frankl really did put it in a book — with the credit attached. What travelled was the sentence; what fell off was the four words after it.

items.why: Goodreads carries the line with the bare attribution “— Victor Frankl” and names no source work at all ↗, which is the form nearly every reposting takes.

Denise Levertov used it as an epigraph in The Freeing of the Dust (1975), citing “Viktor Frankl, The Doctor and the Soul” — correct about the book she took it from, but not noting that Frankl was quoting somebody else ↗. Dozens of later anthologies repeat the Frankl credit without the book.
According to the Wikiquote editor who traced the line, the documentary Jodorowsky’s Dune is among the sources that put Frankl’s name to it ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Frankl never claimed it. His own sentence, in the Winstons’ translation, reads: “‘What is to give light must endure burning,’ Wildgans says ↗. That is, it must suffer.”

context.heading: What the sonnet is actually about
lead: “Helldunkle Stunde” — roughly “chiaroscuro hour” — is a sonnet about dying with the work unfinished. Wildgans opens with the fear that seizes him now and then: that he will die soon and leave behind undone the work a stern design keeps driving him toward. What holds him to life, he says, is not any grasping after pleasure but that unfinished thing.

Then he turns. Life is too restless a surface to hold a reflection of anything that is not itself light. Only what tears away from the flesh flammenhaft — flame-like, in painful and prayerful shaping — can survive as our image. The last line lands as the consequence: whatever is to shine must put up with burning. It is a poet’s statement about the cost of making, written in 1916 by a man who would be dead at fifty-one.
context.detailsSummary: How Frankl used it — and how his name replaced Wildgans’s
detailsBody: Frankl’s use is faithful and openly sourced. In Ärztliche Seelsorge the German runs “…leuchten soll, muß dulden, daß es brennt’, sagt WILDGANS und meint damit wohl: daß es leidet” — says Wildgans, and by that he probably means: that it suffers. The Winstons rendered the same passage in English as “‘What is to give light must endure burning,’ Wildgans says. That is, it must suffer.” Frankl was pressing the poet’s image into service for logotherapy’s claim that suffering can be an achievement rather than a defeat.

The failure mode is ordinary and mechanical. A reader meets a memorable eight-word sentence inside a famous book, copies the sentence, and cites the book’s author. Denise Levertov did the honest version of this in 1975, using the line as an epigraph and citing “Viktor Frankl, The Doctor and the Soul” — accurate about where she found it, silent about the fact that Frankl was quoting. Strip the book title on the next copy and you are left with a bare Frankl credit, which is what Goodreads, the quote aggregators and a thousand social posts now carry.

Worth noting for anyone checking: the line is not in Man’s Search for Meaning, the Frankl book it is most often mentioned alongside. A full text of that book contains neither the sentence nor Wildgans’s name.

sourcesVerified.claim: The poem "Helldunkle Stunde" by Anton Wildgans was written 1916, first published in the collection Mittag (1917), and ends with the line "Was leuchten soll, muß dulden, daß es brennt."
The same closing line appears on p. 183 of Wildgans, Gesammelte Werke, vol. 1 (1930), in the "Gesänge im Mittag" section.

Viktor Frankl's The Doctor and the Soul contains "'What is to give light must endure burning,' Wildgans says.", and Ärztliche Seelsorge contains "Was leuchten soll, muß dulden, daß es brennt', sagt WILDGANS und meint damit wohl: daß es leidet".
Denise Levertov's The Freeing of the Dust carries the line as an epigraph credited to "Viktor Frankl, The Doctor and the Soul"; many other books credit Frankl with no source.
Denise Levertov's The Freeing of the Dust was first published in 1975.

Wikiquote's Talk:Viktor Frankl says the quote is attributed to Frankl by various quotation sites and the documentary Jodorowsky's Dune, but "probably not" his, pointing to Anton Wildgans's 1916 poem Helldunkle Stunde.
Anton Wildgans lived 17 April 1881 – 3 May 1932, was an Austrian poet and playwright, and directed the Burgtheater in 1921–1922 and 1930–1931.
The Doctor and the Soul is the English translation of Ärztliche Seelsorge (1946), translated by Richard and Clara Winston, first published in English by Knopf in 1955.
Goodreads carries the line attributed simply to "Victor Frankl" with no source work named.
Anton Wildgans's collection Mittag has a first publication year of 1917 in library catalog records.
Archive.org's catalog record for the Bantam edition of The Doctor and the Soul credits Richard & Clara Winston as translators.
